extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of classical literature; readers of Montaigne (translated edition)
extracted.subtask_description: A translated selection of Montaigne's essays (end of 'Of Love' and start of 'Of Coaches'), offering moral, political and personal reflections rather than prescriptive formal rules. The page is a literary text intended for readers of essays and classical thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between body and soul in pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing in us purely corporeal or purely spiritual; both body and soul share in pleasures and pains, and neither should be unjustly subordinated to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues it is unjust to treat bodily pleasures as entirely beneath the soul or to treat the soul as a mere servant to the body. The soul should not be made to drag the body along as through servile obligation; rather the soul may invite, regulate, and infuse pleasure into the body so pleasures are sweet and useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of sexual relations by age and condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual/romantic commerce requires relation and correspondence: one should not try to obtain youthful lovers when oneself is old and mismatched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contends it is ridiculous to compete with youthful lovers when old; such pursuits often rely on pity and are degrading. He prefers the contemplation of youth's beauty or suitable matches of like condition. Example aphorism: 'Friend, the hook will not stick in such soft cheese.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer imaginative pleasure over ill-suited physical action
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure given to the imagination by thinking or imagining sometimes exceeds the actual physical pleasure obtained from an ill-suited or degrading union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When physical conditions or reciprocity are lacking, Montaigne values the imaginative or contemplative enjoyment more than seeking a physical act that yields humiliation or disproportionate cost (e.g., being maintained out of pity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject artificial / cosmetically enhanced beauty as object of true love
rubrics_metrics.description: Adulterated, farded, or artificially dressed beauty is unworthy of a wise man's love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote of a young man (Hemon) told by Arcesilaus that a wise man may love provided it be not with a 'farded and adulterated beauty.' Montaigne prefers natural, authentic beauty to polished artificiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate season and timing for love
rubrics_metrics.description: Love and the prime of beauty belong naturally to youthful seasons (the age next to childhood); certain ages are more fitting for love than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes classical authorities (Homer, Plato) and epigrams celebrating adolescence as the proper time for love; he criticizes extending love's authority unduly into later life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love's disorderly nature — rules limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Love frequently ignores rules and order; it is often more graceful under inadvertence and trouble than when guided by art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne observes that love 'ignores rules' and that its charm may be heightened by misadventures and folly; attempts to domesticate it by strict prudence may restrain its 'divine liberty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage requires judgment; fear is not mere absence
rubrics_metrics.description: Being courageous is compatible with recognizing and judging danger; foresight and measured fear are virtues, whereas being astounded or panicked is debilitating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne distinguishes useful foresight from panic. He praises Socrates' calmness in defeat as an example: true courage looks steady at danger, judges it, and organizes retreat or resistance rather than succumbing to astonishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coaches and excessive personal magnificence indicate effeminacy or misplaced dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of coaches, extravagant personal display, and ostentation by princes or private gentlemen can be signs of effeminacy or misunderstanding of their proper dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes monarchs and nobles who seek to appear great by excessive expense (coaches, exotic harnesses), giving historical examples (Marc Antony, Heliogabalus). He finds such displays derogatory when used among one's own subjects or at home.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public expenditure should favor durable public goods over ephemeral magnificence
rubrics_metrics.description: A sovereign's money is better spent on lasting public works (ports, fortifications, churches, hospitals, colleges, roads) than on transient spectacles or personal magnificence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne endorses spending on infrastructures that confer lasting benefit and lasting memory (citing Pope Gregory XIII and Catherine) rather than costly shows that gratify the populace for a moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality of princes must be measured by discretion and merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberality in rulers should be exercised with discretion and regard to merit; indiscriminate or immoderate bounty diminishes respect and utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that a king's liberality, when unmeasured, wastes resources, encourages excessive demands, and can embarrass recipients if given without merit. He quotes Isocrates and Cicero and prefers prudent, well-judged giving (scatter with hand, not pour from sack).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive bounty breeds dependency, ingratitude, and loss of friends
rubrics_metrics.description: When a ruler gives too much or too widely, subjects become excessive in asking, grow less grateful, and the ruler becomes impoverished of true friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne explains that over-generosity makes recipients expect more and not reckon past favours; the more a prince wastes in gifts the poorer he grows in reliable supporters, and he may create servile beneficiaries rather than loyal allies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferring public funds to private entertainments is not genuine liberality
rubrics_metrics.description: Using public money to provide entertainments and extravagances for the people should not count as rightful liberality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Cicero: 'The transferring of money from the right owners to strangers ought not to have the title of liberality.' Montaigne cautions princes who fund public shows at the public's expense, since that merely shows money moved from rightful owners to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer strategic, modest gifts that secure genuine loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: A ruler obtains more faithful support by judicious, relatively small investments in people than by lavish, indiscriminate spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne retells Cyrus' exercise of asking his beneficiaries to lend him sums as a test, showing that well-chosen favors create faithful 'treasurers' of loyalty — a better investment than squandering treasure for spectacle or flattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacles please the baser sort and are fleeting in memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Public spectacles and delights appeal to the lower tastes and vanish from memory once the populace is sated; serious men should not esteem such expenditures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne (following Aristotle and others) critiques the value of games, shows and lavish entertainments as ephemeral pleasures that do not build lasting reputation or civic strength; he gives Probus' gladiatorial displays as an example of grandeur that impresses briefly.
